item.title: Optimizing Evolution Under Cyclic Selection: the Case of B Cells
item.description: arXiv:2610.36596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapid evolutionary adaptation may be necessary for organisms facing strong environmental pressures. Although selection often acts continuously, in the case of B cells evolving high affinity antibodies in germinal centers, selection can take place after multiple rounds of division. To study how the number of divisions between selection events affects adaptation, we develop a minimal computational model of cyclic selection. We find that the optimal average mutation rate per division and the corresponding adaptation velocity are nearly invariant across number of divisions between selections, and we quantitatively explain this behavior with a theory based on the dynamics of the "nose", i.e. the fittest individuals in the population. We also find that when the number of divisions between selection events is large, then mutating every division results in slower adaptation than mutating only at the last division before selection (as is the case for B cells). Our model provides a framework for understanding adaptation in natural and experimental systems subject to cyclic selection.
item.dc:creator: Xingjian Hou, Colin Scheibner, Ned S. Wingreen

item.title: Data-driven stochastic reconstruction of dengue epidemic dynamics: state-dependent stochasticity and temporal organization
item.description: arXiv:2610.36988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dengue epidemics exhibit strong stochastic variability, temporal memory and complex temporal organization that are difficult to capture using conventional deterministic epidemic models. However, the dependence of epidemic fluctuations on the underlying dynamical state and their influence on reconstruction across temporal scales remain insufficiently understood. In this work, we develop a data-driven stochastic framework to investigate dengue epidemic dynamics using daily infection data from Imphal West District, Manipur, India, for 2023-2025. We use Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) to separate deterministic and stochastic epidemic components. Logarithmic regression and autocorrelation analyses reveal empirically state-dependent noise amplitudes and persistent temporal correlations, supporting a phenomenological description involving multiplicative, temporally structures stochasticity. Polynomial and logistic-type drift functions are subsequently fitted to the deterministic components and integrated to reconstruct the epidemic incidence trajectories. Although polynomial drift provides high in-sample agreement with the deterministic dynamics, complexity-entropy analysis reveals that the reconstruction depends on the epidemic year and the embedding delay. A paired circular moving-block bootstrap further demonstrates that observed minimizing delays exhibit different levels of stability across the various reconstructions and years. Finally, we conducted a noise-amplitude sensitivity analysis, and it reveals pronounced changes in the optimal embedding delay and minimum Euclidean distance in the complexity-entropy plane. The proposed framework provides a data-driven approach to characterizing structured stochastic fluctuations and assessing the temporal organization of epidemic dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Tongbram Surkumar Singh, Mairembam Kelvin Singh, Athokpam Langlen Chanu, Moirangthem Shubhakanta Singh

item.title: Multi-day single-cell magnetic imaging of living cancer cells using Quantum Cell Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2610.36359v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Live-cell imaging of cellular and tissue samples relies predominantly on optical modalities, such as fluorescence, confocal, and multiphoton microscopy, in which cellular information is encoded in emitted photons. Photons scatter and attenuate in biological samples, restricting depth resolution, while the excitation light required to produce them induces photodamage that perturbs the very biology under observation. Magnetic fields, by contrast, traverse biological samples without attenuation at cellular length scales, but the imaging modality that extracts the encoded information, magnetic resonance imaging, cannot resolve individual cells. Here we present Quantum Cell Monitoring (QCM), a widefield nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry platform that encodes single-cell information in stray magnetic fields rather than emitted photons and reads it out at subcellular resolution. Integrated with a specialized live-cell incubator, QCM tracks magnetically labeled living cancer for up to 72 h through their individual magnetic field signatures. It captures single-cell mitosis and morphological remodeling, as well as cell cluster formation, splitting, and migration even within dense regions where brightfield contrast collapses. By shifting the carrier of single-cell information from propagating optical photons to static magnetic stray fields, QCM decouples cell from cellular optical accessibility and auto-fluorescence, enabling sustained live-cell observation in regimes inaccessible to optical microscopy.
item.dc:creator: Andre Pointner, Sarah Belasi, Regine Schneider-Stock, Roland Nagy

item.title: Residual dynamics determine dissipation in strongly coupled linear Langevin systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.37030v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Interactions shape the properties of many physical and biological nonequilibrium systems, but whether collective operation raises or lowers entropy production remains difficult to predict. Here, we show that strong coupling suppresses irreversible circulation associated with the directly coupled degrees of freedom. In identical two-dimensional systems, this suppression is monotonic for nonzero coupling modes and guarantees a monotonic decrease of the entropy production rate (EPR), with the corresponding probability currents vanishing in the strong-coupling limit. In higher dimensions, suppressing the circulation associated with the coupled degrees of freedom does not generally eliminate all irreversible circulation, since the remaining degrees of freedom can still sustain nonequilibrium currents. The EPR of these residual dynamics sets the strong-coupling limit, providing a criterion for whether a given choice of coupled variables leads to lower dissipation than the uncoupled system. The approach to this limit depends on how the finite-coupling current correction aligns with the residual current. Further, we show that convergence to residual dynamics in the strong-coupling limit also applies to coupled non-identical systems. Finally, we demonstrate the predicted EPR reduction in nonlinear models of vertebrate hair-cell bundles and bacterial chemotaxis.
item.dc:creator: Vansh Kharbanda, Anton F. Burnet, Benedikt Sabass

item.title: Thermal scaling laws for open-water swimming
item.description: arXiv:2608.20719v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Open-water swimming defines a thermal phase-boundary problem in which metabolic heat production competes with environmental heat loss. We derive a scaling law that predicts the critical water temperature and shows how body size, swim pace, and insulation shift this boundary. Longitudinal warm- and cold-water data reveal transient dynamics that exceed single-compartment predictions, but emerge naturally from core--peripheral physiology. Together, our results suggest that thermal safety depends on swimmer-specific characteristics and swimming conditions, not on water temperature alone.
item.dc:creator: Henry van den Bedem, Ellen Kuhl

item.title: Active tissue mechanics drives a diversity of collective flows in uniaxially compressed 3D spheroids
item.description: arXiv:2610.24959v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Compression can enhance or suppress cell motion and induce coherent rotation in tissue spheroids, but the physical factors governing these responses remain unclear. Using a minimal three-dimensional active vertex model, we examine how tissue mechanics, active driving, and directional alignment shape the response to uniaxial compression. Without alignment, compression enhances transverse motion in solid-like spheroids throughout the tested activity range, whereas fluid-like spheroids switch from acceleration at low activity to slowing at high activity. Changes in contact persistence connect these responses to neighbor exchange. Passive five-cell calculations show that compression reshapes local rearrangement barriers depending on geometry and loading direction; a high-strain increase in the fluid-like mean coexists with many low-barrier paths. With strong alignment, compression induces coherent rotation in solid-like spheroids, while fluid-like spheroids show no comparable rotation. Rotating solids retain more persistent cell contacts than fluids and develop tangential organization of peripheral cells. Controlled perturbations reveal that compression softens a differential-twist mode and activity slows its relaxation. Together, these results link activity-dependent reversal of the speed response and compression-induced coherent rotation to contact dynamics, local rearrangement costs, and active driving. Our findings demonstrate that one minimal model, with parameters representing effective mechanical and active tissue properties, captures diverse collective responses to compression and provides a framework for predicting how different tissues respond to mechanical loading.
item.dc:creator: Liyang Wang, Shabeeb Ameen, J. M. Schwarz, Tao Zhang

item.title: mdRNAcat: A Molecular Dynamics RNA Catalog of REST2 Conformational Ensembles
item.description: arXiv:2610.35204v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning molecular models of RNA requires simulation data that capture conformational variability and provide consistent physical training signals. Here, we introduce mdRNAcat, a curated dataset of all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of 48 RNA systems selected to promote sequence diversity. Each system is simulated using replica-exchange with solute scaling (REST2), with 32 Hamiltonian states and production lengths of 200-300 ns per state. The dataset provides atomic coordinates, instantaneous forces, and forces reevaluated under the unscaled reference Hamiltonian, together with structural annotations and replica-exchange metadata. Coordinates and forces are available at 1 ps intervals for the reference state and 100 ps intervals across all states in a standardized HDF5 format. We characterize conformational sampling, exchange behavior, base pairing, and sugar-pucker distributions to document the properties of the simulated ensembles. mdRNAcat provides a reusable resource for developing and evaluating data-driven RNA models, including coarse-grained force fields.
item.dc:creator: Anton E. Dorn, Emile de Bruyn, Fabrice von der Lehr, Philipp Knechtges, Stefan Kesselheim, Alexander Schug
